item.title: How do I get my Instagram DMs ready for Black Friday?
item.dc:creator: Chinenye
item.description: Write down your offer and the questions buyers will ask, then write your answers once. Add a checkout link and a backup payment option, set up a way to send the answers without you, and test it with messy messages. Black Friday is on 27 November this year, so start now.
item.content:encoded:
Black Friday does not test your product. It tests your inbox.

Your price may be good. Your photos may be good. But when the messages start coming in, one thing decides the sale: can you answer while the buyer is still interested?

Black Friday is on 27 November this year. That sounds far away. It is not, if you want to do this properly.

What changes on Black Friday

More messages. The same questions. And buyers who want an answer now, because the next seller is one tap away.

Say you run a small shoe brand. On a normal week you get a handful of messages a day, and you answer them between other jobs. On Black Friday the same questions arrive all at once: "How much is this one?", "Is it still available?", "Does the sale cover this?", "When will it arrive?"

You know every answer. The problem is not knowledge. It is typing the same thing a hundred times while the next buyer waits.

Write your offer down first

Before you write one answer, write your offer in one place. What is on sale. What is not. When it ends. Your last day for delivery.

Do this on paper or in a note, not in your head. If it only lives in your head, you will answer the same question two different ways at 11 PM.

Then write the questions

Open your last busy week of messages and copy out every question. If you have no history, ask a friend to message you as a buyer would.

You will notice something. It is the same ten questions, in different words.

Write the answers yourself

Your answers should sound like you. Short. Clear. With the price, the delivery time and the next step.

This matters even if a system sends them for you. The system sends your words, not its own guesses.

Two ways to pay

Add your checkout link. Then add a backup, like bank transfer details, for the buyer whose card fails. Do not wait until someone is stuck at the payment step to think about it.

Test it with messy messages

Real buyers type like real people. "Price pls." "Abeg, is it available?" Half sentences. Typos.

Send your setup ten bad messages before the sale. If it breaks on one, fix the answer, not the buyer.

Decide what happens when it does not know

No setup answers everything. So decide ahead of time what happens when a buyer asks something you did not plan for.

The simplest answer is honest. Tell them you will reply properly in the morning, and save the message so you can. That is better than a wrong answer, and far better than silence.

The steps

  1. Write down your offer. What is on sale, what is not, when it ends, your delivery cut-off.
  2. List the questions buyers will ask. Copy them from your real messages.
  3. Write your answer to each one. Short, clear, in your voice.
  4. Add your checkout link and a backup payment option.
  5. Set up a way to send the answers without you. A system that reads the whole message, not a menu of buttons.
  6. Test it with ten messy messages. Fix anything that breaks.
  7. Decide what happens when it does not know.
  8. Check it once more the week before. Not the night before.

If you want to understand how this works first, you can book a one-on-one consultation. If you want it built for your business, see how the DM system works.

I would rather spend an afternoon on this now than lose sales in the middle of the sale.

item.title: How do I turn one idea into a week of posts?
item.dc:creator: Chinenye
item.description: Start with one lesson you already teach, in three to six sentences. Give it to an AI tool with your voice and a rule not to invent anything, and ask for one newsletter, three short captions and three hooks. Edit them, add one real example, and spread them across your week.
item.content:encoded:
You do not have a content problem. You have one good lesson and no time.

That is usually the whole story. You know something useful. You have said it to a client, in a voice note, in a DM. But when it is time to post, you stare at the screen and start from zero.

So here is a better way to start.

Start with a lesson, not a topic

A topic is "bookkeeping". A lesson is "keep one account for your business and nothing else".

The tool cannot make up your lesson for you. It can only reshape what you give it. Thin input gives thin posts. So the first job is yours: write or say one lesson you really teach, in three to six sentences.

Say you run a bookkeeping service for small shops. Your lesson might be: "Most owners mix business and personal spending in one account. Then at the end of the month nobody knows what the shop really earned. I tell them to open a separate account and move only what they pay themselves." That is a view, a rule and a reason. It is enough to work with.

If typing feels slow, speak it into a voice note and turn it into text. Your own rhythm is in there.

What you ask for

You are not asking for a week of posts. You are asking for a small set of things that come from one idea:

  • one newsletter draft
  • three short captions
  • three hook options for a short video

Give the tool your lesson, tell it to use your voice and plain words, and tell it not to invent stories, numbers or client results. That last rule matters more than the rest.

Where the week comes from

This is the part people miss. One lesson, cut three ways, fills a week without repeating yourself.

A caption on Monday states the rule. A short video on Wednesday opens with a hook and shows the mistake. The newsletter on Friday tells the longer story. Same idea. Different shape each time.

Edit before you post

Do not skip this.

Read each piece out loud. Cross out anything you would never say to a friend. Cross out any claim you have not really made. Then add one real example from a real client or a real day, because that is the line no tool can write for you.

Three ways this goes wrong

You paste a topic. "Bookkeeping" gives you a brochure. A lesson gives you a post.

You post it as it came. The first version is a rough cut. Treat it like one.

You let it add a story. If it did not happen, it does not go in. A made-up result costs you far more than a quiet week.

The steps

  1. Pick one lesson you already teach. Not a topic. A lesson.
  2. Write or speak it in three to six sentences.
  3. Paste it in with your voice and your rules. Plain words, and no invented stories, numbers or results.
  4. Ask for a newsletter draft, three short captions and three hook options.
  5. Edit all of it. Cross out what you would not say. Add one real example.
  6. Spread it across your week. Caption first, video in the middle, newsletter at the end.
  7. Post one edited hook and watch the response. Change one thing next time and compare.

The full setup, with the prompt and the test checklist, is in the Create layer of the Starter Kit. This post is the reason it works.

I would rather post one lesson three ways than three half-ideas once.

item.title: What happens to my Black Friday ad spend if I reply too slowly?
item.dc:creator: Chinenye
item.description: Your ads keep spending whether or not anyone answers. If a buyer messages and waits, you have paid for the click and lost the sale. Fix your reply speed first, so every message gets an answer in seconds, even when you are asleep, and only then raise your budget.
item.content:encoded:
Meta does not care that your phone battery is dead.

Your ads keep running. Your budget keeps spending. And the buyer who clicked, got curious and sent you a message is now sitting there, waiting.

That is the whole problem with Black Friday ad spend. It is not that the ads fail. It is that they work, and then nobody answers.

Where the money leaks

Picture it. You raise your budget before the sale. Messages start coming in at night. You are asleep, the power is out, or you are busy with another customer.

You paid for that click. You got the message. And you made no sale.

There are three places this usually leaks:

  • The first reply is slow. The buyer waits, gets tired, and messages someone else.
  • You type the same answers by hand. At volume, you cannot keep up, and the replies get later and shorter.
  • Payment gets in the way. The card fails, the buyer has no other option, and they leave.

None of this is about your product or your price. It is about what happens after the click.

Fix the reply first

Here is the order that makes sense. Fix the reply, then raise the budget. Not the other way round.

More budget sends you more messages. If you cannot answer the ones you already get, you will pay more for more silence.

This is also why a phone is a weak place to keep your replies. Your battery, your network and your power are all in the chain. Moving the replies to a server takes the weakest part out.

Check where you stand today

Open your last twenty messages. For each one, note how long the buyer waited for a first answer. Mark the ones that never got one.

Do not skip this. It tells you what the leak actually is, and most people are surprised by what they find.

What a good first reply does

A good first reply is not clever. It does three things.

It answers the question the buyer actually asked. It gives the next step, like the checkout link. And it sounds like you, not like a form letter.

Do those three things quickly and you keep the buyer. Miss any of them and the buyer goes back to scrolling. And on Black Friday, scrolling is the competition.

The steps

  1. Check how long a buyer waits for a first reply today. Use your last twenty messages.
  2. Mark the messages that got no reply at all. That is your leak.
  3. Write your answers to the questions that come up most. Price, delivery, availability, payment.
  4. Set up a way to send them without you. One that reads the whole message and runs on a server, not your phone.
  5. Add your checkout link and a backup payment option. If a card fails, the buyer should see another way to pay straight away.
  6. Save the buyer's contact details before you send the link. Then you can follow up.
  7. Test it with messy messages. Typos, slang, half sentences.
  8. Only then raise your budget.

If you want to understand your own leak first, you can book a one-on-one consultation. If you want the replies built for your business, see how the DM system works.

Spend on the ad after you have fixed the answer. Not before.

item.title: What should I do before Black Friday as an online seller?
item.dc:creator: Chinenye
item.description: Decide your offer and count your stock first. Then test your payment and delivery, plan your content, get your DM answers ready, and run one full test the week before. Black Friday is on 27 November this year, so start now and work in order.
item.content:encoded:
Do not start with the ads. Start with the boring list.

Most Black Friday trouble does not come from a bad offer. It comes from small things nobody checked: a checkout link that fails, a delivery date nobody confirmed, a stock count that was wrong. These are all things you can fix now, while it is quiet.

Black Friday is on 27 November this year. Work through this list in order.

Now: decide your offer and count your stock

Say you run a small bag brand. The first job is not a photo or a caption. It is a note that says what is on sale, what is not, when it ends and your last day for delivery.

  • Write down your offer in one place
  • Check your numbers, so you do not sell at a loss
  • Count your stock, item by item
  • Decide what you will do when something sells out

Everything else depends on this note. Your ads, your captions and your replies will all repeat it.

Four weeks out: test payment and delivery

This is the step people skip, and it is the one that costs the most on the day.

  • Buy something from your own checkout, start to finish
  • Add a backup way to pay, like bank transfer details, for when a card fails
  • Confirm you can see every payment as it lands
  • Ask your delivery partner what they can handle on a busy day, and set your delivery cut-off from their answer

If something breaks here, you have weeks to fix it. If it breaks on Black Friday, you have minutes.

Two weeks out: plan your content and ready your DMs

You will be busy that week. So write your posts before it starts.

  • Plan the posts for the whole week, including a few teasers before the sale
  • Write the answers to the questions buyers will ask
  • Set up a way to send those answers without you
  • Decide what happens when a buyer asks something you did not plan for

For the content, you can plan a month in one sitting, and the Create layer of the Starter Kit is built for that. For the messages, read how to get your DMs ready, then check what slow replies cost your ad spend before you raise any budget.

The week of: run a full test, then plan to rest

  • Send your setup ten messy messages: typos, slang, half sentences
  • Walk through the buyer's whole path one more time, from message to payment
  • Decide who answers what, and when you will sleep

That last one matters more than it sounds. A tired seller makes slow, short replies. Plan your rest the way you plan your stock.

After: follow up

Black Friday does not end when the sale does.

  • Thank the people who bought
  • Write to the people who messaged and did not buy
  • Write down what worked while you still remember it

The people who asked about your product are the warmest list you will have all year. Do not let them go cold.

The steps, in short

  1. Write your offer down and count your stock.
  2. Test your checkout and your backup payment.
  3. Confirm delivery and set your cut-off.
  4. Plan your content and your DM answers.
  5. Run a full test the week before.
  6. Plan your rest.
  7. Follow up after.

If you want a second pair of eyes on how your business runs before the rush, you can book a one-on-one consultation. If you want your replies handled while you sleep, see how the DM system works.

Do the boring list now. The sale takes care of itself after that.

item.title: How do I know which tasks in my business to automate first?
item.dc:creator: Chinenye
item.description: Start with the task you repeat most that needs no real thinking. Write down what you actually do for one week, then pick the one that eats the most time. Automate that one, test it, and only then pick the next.
item.content:encoded:
Do not start with the tool. Start with the task.

Most people do it the other way round. They hear about a new tool, get excited, and go looking for something to point it at. Three weeks later it is sitting there, half set up, and nothing has changed.

So here is a better order.

Picture a normal Tuesday. You answer the same three questions in your DMs. You copy a customer's details into a sheet. You type the same payment details again for someone new. By evening you have done a lot, and none of it grew the business.

And the question you would ask is: which of those do I fix first?

Look at where the hours leak

There are four places time usually leaks in a small business.

  • Lead capture and tracking. Someone shows interest and their details end up nowhere.
  • Manual work and repeated admin. The same copy, paste and retype, every day.
  • Data storage and security. Customer details sitting in places you would not want to explain.
  • Platform and audience risk. Your whole audience lives on one app you do not own.

You do not need to fix all four. You need to see which one is costing you most.

Pick the boring one

The best first task to automate is boring. You repeat it often, it needs no real thinking, and you would not miss doing it.

The worst first task is the one that needs your judgement. A difficult customer. A price you have to decide on the spot. Leave those with you.

Say you sell fabric online. Your week list might look like this: answering "is this still available?" in your DMs, sending the same delivery details to every buyer, copying each order into a sheet, posting on Instagram, choosing new stock, and calming a buyer who got the wrong colour.

Cross out choosing new stock and the wrong-colour complaint. Both need your judgement. What is left is repeat work. Of those, the DM questions and the delivery details come back every single day, so they cost you the most time.

That is your first task. Not the clever one. The one that keeps coming back.

Why one at a time

It is tempting to fix everything in one weekend. Please do not.

When you automate one task, you learn how it behaves. Where it breaks. What it does with a typo or a half-finished message. When you automate five, you learn none of that, and you will not know which one is causing the problem.

There is also trust. You will only let a system run unwatched once you have seen it get the small things right. That takes a few days of checking it yourself. Do that for one task before you add another.

The steps

  1. Write down what you actually do for one week. Not what you think you do. Keep a running list.
  2. Mark everything you repeat. If you did it more than twice, mark it.
  3. Cross out anything that needs your judgement. That stays with you.
  4. Pick the one that costs the most time. Only one.
  5. Set it up, then test it with messy input. Typos, half sentences, odd requests. If it breaks, fix the setup before you trust it.
  6. Move to the next one only when the first one holds.

It sounds slow. It is faster than setting up five things and trusting none of them.

If you want a worksheet for the first step, the free AutoStack Checklist is called Get Your Lost Hours Back. You can get it here.

Pick the boring task. It is never the exciting one that gives you your hours back.

item.title: How do I reply to Instagram DMs at night without staying awake?
item.dc:creator: Chinenye
item.description: Set up an automated DM system that reads the customer's actual message, answers it, and sends the checkout link. It runs on a server, not your phone, so a flat battery or a power cut does not stop it. You write the answers. The system delivers them.
item.content:encoded:
Most business owners answer DMs at night because they are scared of losing the sale. I get it.

But think about what that costs you.

Picture it. A customer sees your ad late at night. She asks if she can pay in two parts. Your phone is on 4%, the power is out, and you are asleep. She waits a while, then messages someone else.

That is the problem. It is not that you are lazy. A person cannot be awake all night, and your ad does not stop running when you sleep.

Why the usual fix does not work

The usual fix is a comment-to-DM button. Someone comments a word, a menu pops up, and they tap a number.

It works until a customer types a normal sentence. Or a typo. Or slang. Then the menu does not know what to do, and the customer is talking to a wall.

And the question you would ask is: so what is the better way?

What to set up instead

You want a system that reads the message the way a person would. It answers the question, then moves the customer to checkout. It has to live on a server, so it does not depend on your phone, your battery or your generator.

Say you run a fashion brand. The messages you get most are probably: "How much is this one?", "Is it available?", "Do you deliver to Abuja?", "How long will delivery take?" and "Can I pay half now?"

You already know the answers. The system's job is to send them, in your words, the moment the message lands. For "Can I pay half now?", it sends your payment plan and then the checkout link. For "Do you deliver to Abuja?", it answers and asks which item they want.

The customer gets a reply while they are still looking. You wake up to a sale, not an apology.

Decide what happens when it does not know

No system answers everything. So decide, before you switch it on, what happens when a customer asks something you did not plan for.

The simplest answer is honest. The system tells the customer you will reply in the morning, saves the message, and you pick it up when you wake. That is far better than a made-up answer, or silence.

This is also the part people skip. They test the easy questions, see it work, and go to sleep. Then the odd question comes in at 2 AM.

Why your phone should not be the system

If your customer chats live on your own phone, you depend on your battery, your network and your power. A flat phone, a light out, a generator that is not running, and your sales funnel goes quiet while your ad keeps spending.

Moving the replies to a server is not about being fancy. It is about taking the weakest part, your phone, out of the chain.

The steps

  1. Write down the ten questions customers ask most. Price, delivery, payment plans, refunds. Your own inbox already has them.
  2. Write the answer to each one yourself. The system sends your words, not its own guesses.
  3. Connect your checkout link and a backup payment option. If a card fails, the customer should see another way to pay right away.
  4. Save the customer's contact details before sending the link. Then you can follow up later.
  5. Test it with messy messages. Typos, half sentences, the way people really type. If it breaks, fix the answer, not the customer.

Do not rush step five. This is where most setups fail, and it is the cheapest place to catch it.

If you want to understand it first, you can book a one-on-one consultation. If you want it built for your business, see how the DM system works.

I would rather spend an hour setting this up once than lose a sale every night.

item.title: Starter Kit or Blueprint: which one should I buy?
item.dc:creator: Chinenye
item.description: Buy the Starter Kit if you want AI to do real work in your business and you do not use n8n. Buy the Blueprint if you build with n8n and want 50 ready workflows. If you are not sure, start with the free Checklist.
item.content:encoded:
Do not buy both because they look good together. Buy the one that matches how you work.

One question settles most of it: do you build with n8n?

If the answer is no, look at the Starter Kit. If the answer is yes, look at the Blueprint. The rest of this post is why.

The Starter Kit is for people who want AI to do real work

It is for business owners, creators and operators. You do not need to build anything, and you do not need n8n.

The kit is a workspace of ready-to-run setups. One setup is one card. Each card has one pain, one outcome, the steps, a prompt, a test checklist and the limits. There are 36 of them, in four layers: Ask, Create, Automate and Edit. It starts with Claude, and community access is included.

Say you run a small food business. You post on Instagram, you answer the same questions all day, and you never have time. A setup that turns one idea into a week of posts is for you. So is one that handles messages you keep repeating.

The Blueprint is for people who build

It is for builders, VAs and do-it-yourself operators who already use n8n.

The Blueprint gives you 50 ready workflows for your leads, your invoices and your daily admin. It also comes with a client pitch script and a commercial license.

Say you are a VA who sets up systems for clients. You do not want to build every workflow from nothing. Fifty ready ones give you a start, and the pitch script helps you offer them to clients.

One small naming note

A setup and a blueprint are not the same thing. A setup is a card inside the Starter Kit. A blueprint is an n8n file inside the Blueprint. If someone tells you they "bought the blueprint", ask which product they mean.

The steps

  1. Ask yourself one question. Do I build with n8n?
  2. If no, start with the Starter Kit. It is built for people who want AI to do the work without building anything.
  3. If yes, and you build for yourself or for clients, look at the Blueprint.
  4. If you only want to see if this is for you, take the free Checklist first. You can get it here.
  5. Pick one. Add the other only when the first one is running.

You can read more on the Starter Kit page and the Blueprint page.

Buy the one you will open this week. The one that sits unopened helps nobody.

item.title: Why does everything I write with AI sound like AI?
item.dc:creator: Chinenye
item.description: Because AI can only reshape what you give it. Give it a thin idea and it hands back a thin, generic post. Feed it your own words, your own example and a few plain rules, then edit what comes back before you post.
item.content:encoded:
Your AI does not sound like you because you did not give it you.

That is the whole answer. The rest of this post is how to fix it.

Here is what usually happens. You open Claude or ChatGPT and type: "Write me a post about time management." The tool has nothing of yours to work with. So it reaches for the average of everything it has read. Polite. Tidy. A bit like a brochure.

You read it and think, who wrote this?

And the question you would ask is: so how do I make it sound like me?

Start with your own words, not an empty box

An AI tool can only reshape what you give it. Thin input gives thin posts.

So give it something real. One lesson you teach, in three to six sentences. If typing feels slow, speak it into a voice note and paste the transcript. Your rhythm is in there. Your odd little phrases too.

Say you coach freelancers on pricing. Here is the thin version you might type: "Write a post about pricing."

Here is the real version: "Most freelancers price by guessing what the client can afford. I price by how long the work takes and what it has to cover. If a client says it is too much, I do not drop the price. I drop the scope."

The first gives the tool nothing to hold on to. The second gives it a view, a rule and a reason. Same tool. Very different post.

Tell it your rules

Most of the "AI sound" is habits. Long sentences. Words nobody says out loud. Neat little lists of three adjectives. Cheerful endings that wrap everything up.

Write your rules once and paste them in with every request. Plain words. Short sentences. No invented stories, numbers or client results. Say the thing, then stop.

Now you want to know if the rules matter that much. They do. Without them the tool goes back to its defaults, and its defaults are what you are trying to escape.

Edit like it is your own draft

This part is not optional.

Read what comes back out loud. Anything you would never say to a friend, cross it out. Anything that sounds too sure about a result you have not had, cross it out. What is left is closer to you than anything you could get in one click.

Then add your own example from a real client or a real day. That is the line no tool can write for you, and it is the line people remember.

Four mistakes that make it worse

Asking for everything at once. One request for a newsletter, ten captions and a video script gets you one flat blob. Ask for less and you get more of you.

Pasting a topic instead of a lesson. "Productivity" is a topic. "Why I stopped checking my phone before I wrote" is a lesson. The tool needs the second one.

Taking the first draft. The first draft is a rough cut. Treat it like one.

Letting it add stories. If a story did not happen, it should not be in your post. Say so in your rules, in plain words, every time.

I know it feels slower than clicking once. But the post you edit for ten minutes is the post people reply to, and the one you click once is the one they scroll past.

The steps

  1. Write or speak one lesson you teach. Three to six sentences is enough.
  2. Paste it in with your rules. Ask for your voice, plain words, and no invented stories, numbers or results.
  3. Read the result out loud. Cross out anything you would never say.
  4. Add one real example. A real client or a real day, never a made-up one.
  5. Post one version and watch the response. Change one hook next time and compare.

The full setup for this is in the Starter Kit, in the Create layer. This post is only the reason it works.

I would rather post something plain that sounds like me than something polished that sounds like nobody.
